outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the best known lower bound for the classical Bloch constant B rose from √3/4 + 2·10⁻⁴ to √3/4 + 0.0153 ≈ 0.448313 (Frank Wikström, arXiv 2608.17660, posted 18 Aug 2026, unrefereed, with a disclosed AI-tool statement), and the best known lower bound for the classical Landau constant L rose to L > 0.51 (Wikström, arXiv 2609.23236, posted 19 Sep 2026, computer-assisted, with a similar AI-tool statement); neither exact value is known, both upper bounds (≈0.4718617 for B, ≈0.5432589 for L) are unchanged, and I found no independent public engagement with either paper.
problem_asks: The statement asks for the exact values of 'Landau's constants' and of 'Bloch's constant', read as follows. (a) Bloch's constant B: the optimal radius in Bloch's theorem, i.e. the infimum over holomorphic f on the unit disk with f'(0)=1 of the radius of the largest univalent (schlicht) disk contained in f(D). Exact value requested; no bound, no approximation. (b) Landau's constant L: the infimum over the same class of the radius of the largest disk contained in f(D), univalence not required. Exact value requested. (c) The plural 'Landau's constants' is read here as also covering the injective (univalent) Bloch–Landau constant A, defined over injective holomorphic f on the unit disk with f'(0)=1, which the Wikipedia-style 'Landau constants' text lists alongside L and B. The statement does not name A; this is a reading, flagged for the judging pass. (d) Not included on my reading: Landau's G_n coefficient sums (Cvijović–Srivastava), a different family that shares the name. Also flagged. The problem therefore has three parts (a), (b), (c), each asking for an exact value. A bound moving on any of them is not a settlement of that part.

events.what_happened: L. Ahlfors, 'An extension of Schwarz's lemma', Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 43 (1938) 359–364. Per the reference list and introduction of arXiv 2608.17660, Ahlfors obtained the lower bound B ≥ √3/4 for Bloch's constant. Per arXiv 2609.23236's introduction, the same paper gives L ≥ 1/2 (the introduction renders this as 'B≥3/4' in the sentence about the extension, which I read as a rendering of √3/4 and did not verify). The Ahlfors paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Lower bounds B ≥ √3/4 ≈ 0.4330 (classical Bloch constant) and L ≥ 1/2 (classical Landau constant). Both are for the classical class.
events.remains: Parts (a), (b), (c) all open; these are the historical starting bounds for the later improvements.

checked_by.who: Transactions of the American Mathematical Society (journal of record)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper; the publication is attested by the reference list of arXiv 2608.17660, not by my reading of the paper

events.direction: Lower bounds, in the direction of the eventual exact values lying above these.

events.what_happened: M. Heins, 'On a class of conformal metrics', Nagoya Math. J. (1961), which strengthens the Ahlfors–Schwarz lemma; a search snippet states that Heins used the strict form of the inequality to show that B is strictly greater than √3/4, without giving an explicit increment. This is from a search-result snippet of the Nagoya paper's listing and of an Encyclopedia-style summary; I did not open the Heins paper.
events.delivers: Strict inequality B > √3/4 for the classical Bloch constant; no numerical increment.
events.remains: Parts (a), (b), (c) all open; no exact value.
events.doubts: Recorded from a search snippet only; the Heins paper was not opened.
events.direction: Strict lower bound, in the same direction as Ahlfors's.

events.what_happened: L. Ahlfors and H. Grunsky, 'Über die Blochsche Konstante', Math. Z. 42 (1937) 671–673. They gave the upper bound B ≤ Γ(1/3)Γ(11/12)/(Γ(1/4)√(1+√3)) ≈ 0.4718617 and conjectured that this is the exact value of B. Wikipedia's Bloch-theorem article also credits them with the conjecture that their upper bound for L is its exact value; MathWorld and the Rademacher line credit the L upper bound to Robinson and Rademacher instead (see disputes). The Ahlfors–Grunsky paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Upper bound B ≤ 0.4718617… for the classical Bloch constant, with the conjecture that it equals B. The conjecture is the open problem for part (a).
events.remains: Part (a): the exact value of B is conjectured to be this upper bound and remains unproved. Parts (b) and (c) not addressed by this paper as cited.
events.direction: Upper bound, with the conjecture that it is sharp. Sharpness is what remains open.
events.object: An extremal-type holomorphic function, which the 1937 paper uses to constrain B from above; the function is not described in the sources I read.

events.what_happened: H. Rademacher, 'On the Bloch–Landau constant', Amer. J. Math. 65 (1943) 387–390, publishing the upper bound L ≤ Γ(1/3)Γ(5/6)/Γ(1/6) ≈ 0.5432589 and conjecturing equality. MathWorld credits the same bound to R. Robinson (1938), whose argument was unpublished; I date the event to the first public written argument, which is the 1943 paper.
events.revisions: Robinson (1938) unpublished; Rademacher (1943) first public written argument.
events.delivers: Upper bound L ≤ 0.5432589… for the classical Landau constant, with the conjecture that it equals L.
events.remains: Part (b): exact value of L, conjectured to equal the upper bound, unproved. Parts (a) and (c) not addressed.
events.direction: Upper bound with the conjecture of sharpness, which remains open.

events.what_happened: M. Bonk, 'On Bloch's constant', Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 110 (1990) 889–894, giving B ≥ √3/4 + 10⁻¹⁴, the first quantitative improvement on Ahlfors's √3/4. Per MathWorld and the Wikström introduction. The Bonk paper itself was not opened; the 1988 thesis is also mentioned in one snippet.
events.delivers: Lower bound B ≥ √3/4 + 10⁻¹⁴ for the classical Bloch constant.
events.remains: Part (a): exact value of B open.
events.direction: Lower bound, in the direction of the eventual exact value.

events.what_happened: H. Chen and P. M. Gauthier, 'On Bloch's constant', J. Anal. Math. 69 (1996) 275–291, refining Bonk's method to B ≥ √3/4 + 2·10⁻⁴. Per the Wikström introduction and the Bloch-theorem article (which credits them with the lower bound). The Chen–Gauthier paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Lower bound B ≥ √3/4 + 2·10⁻⁴ for the classical Bloch constant. This was the record immediately before 18 Aug 2026.
events.remains: Part (a): exact value of B open.
events.direction: Lower bound, in the direction of the eventual exact value.

events.what_happened: C. Xiong, 'Lower bound of Bloch's constant', Nanjing Daxue Xuebao Shuxue Bannian Kan 15 (1998) 174–179. Per Wikström's introduction, Xiong gave B ≥ √3/4 + 3·10⁻⁴. Wikström states that he could not obtain Xiong's paper and took the value from a MathSciNet quotation and a zbMath review. MathWorld and ProofWiki-style sources instead attribute the √3/4 + 2·10⁻⁴ figure to Chen–Gauthier and list Xiong 1998 among the subsequent refinements. Not opened.
events.delivers: Claimed lower bound B ≥ √3/4 + 3·10⁻⁴ for the classical Bloch constant; the figure itself is unverified, see doubts.
events.remains: Part (a): exact value of B open.
events.doubts: The value √3/4 + 3·10⁻⁴ is the author's quotation from MathSciNet/zbMath, not checked against the paper (which was not obtained by the 2026 author). MathWorld attributes the 2·10⁻⁴ figure to Chen–Gauthier and Xiong together. The two accounts disagree about which value Xiong proved.
events.direction: Lower bound, in the direction of the eventual exact value.

events.what_happened: K. Yanagihara, 'On the locally univalent Bloch constant', J. Anal. Math. 65 (1995) 1–17. Sources disagree about which constant the bound concerns. Eremenko's Purdue notes, a 2023 Canadian Mathematical Bulletin paper and a 2026 survey snippet give L > 1/2 + 10⁻³³⁵ for the Landau constant. Wikström's arXiv 2609.23236 introduction says Yanagihara proved B∞ > 1/2 + 10⁻⁴¹⁷ for the locally univalent Bloch constant. The paper itself was not opened; the Purdue notes were not opened (PDF).
events.delivers: A bound just above 1/2 for one of the two constants, depending on the source: L > 1/2 + 10⁻³³⁵ (Purdue notes, Bhowmik–Sen snippet) or B∞ > 1/2 + 10⁻⁴¹⁷ (Wikström 2609.23236). The locally univalent B∞ is a variant of the classical B, not the classical B itself.
events.remains: Part (b): exact value of L open. Part (a) open.
events.doubts: Attribution conflict between sources: 10⁻³³⁵ for L versus 10⁻⁴¹⁷ for B∞. Not resolved from the sources I could read.
events.direction: Lower bound, in the direction of the eventual exact value.

events.what_happened: H. Chen and T. Shiba (year 2004 per a 2026 survey snippet), who improved a lower bound to 1/2 + 2·10⁻⁸ by 'refining the escaping-path geometry'. Wikström's arXiv 2609.23236 introduction assigns this bound to the locally univalent Bloch constant B∞; other snippets assign it to L. The Chen–Shiba paper was not opened.
events.delivers: B∞ > 1/2 + 2·10⁻⁸ per Wikström's introduction, which is a variant (locally univalent) constant; per other snippets, L > 1/2 + 2·10⁻⁸. Attribution conflict, see disputes.
events.doubts: Attribution to B∞ or L differs across sources; the year 2004 comes from a search snippet, not the paper.

events.what_happened: T. Carroll and J. Ortega-Cerdà, 'The univalent Bloch–Landau constant, harmonic symmetry and conformal glueing', arXiv:0806.2282 (first posted 13 June 2008), published J. Math. Pures Appl. 92 (2009) 396–406. Improves the upper bound for the univalent (injective) Bloch–Landau constant A using a modified Goodman domain and Fedorov's solution of the Pólya–Chebotarev problem for four symmetric points. The numerical value 0.6563937 is taken from a survey snippet and a MaRDI entry; the abstract does not state it, and I did not open the full paper.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 13 Jun 2008; journal version J. Math. Pures Appl. 92 (2009) 396–406.
events.delivers: Upper bound for the univalent (injective) constant A, improved to about 0.6564 from the 0.7853 figure in the Wikipedia-style Landau-constants text. This is a restatement of A's upper bound, not of the classical L or B. Its inclusion in the problem depends on the reading in problem_asks (c).
events.remains: Part (c): exact value of A open; the classical L and B are not addressed.

checked_by.who: Journal of Mathematics Pures et Appliquées (journal of record)

events.direction: Upper bound for A moves downward, consistent with A being a constant below its own upper bound.

events.what_happened: Lower bound A > 0.5708858 for the univalent constant, attributed to Skinner in 2009, after Zhang–Jenkins (> 0.57088) and earlier bounds from Reich, Jenkins and Toppila. Recorded from a search-result summary of the Carroll–Ortega-Cerdà survey and a 2023 Bhowmik–Sen snippet; no page was opened for this item.

events.remains: Part (c): exact value of A open.
events.doubts: Snippet-only attribution; not verified against the original Skinner paper.

events.what_happened: B. Bhowmik and S. Sen, 'Landau-type Theorem and Bloch constant for elliptic harmonic mappings', arXiv:2404.04596, submitted 6 April 2024. Proves a Landau-type theorem and a Bloch-type radius bound for (K,K')-elliptic harmonic mappings.
events.delivers: Lower bound on a radius for (K,K')-elliptic harmonic mappings with an explicit formula ρ₁ = 1/√2 + ... ln(t/(1+t)). A variant: harmonic, elliptic class. It does not touch the classical holomorphic B or L; the paper quotes the classical bounds only as background.
events.remains: Parts (a), (b), (c) of the statement all unaffected.
events.direction: Variant result; does not cut against the classical conjectures.

events.what_happened: H. Hamada, G. Kohr, M. Kohr, 'Bieberbach conjecture, Bohr radius, Bloch constant and Alexander's theorem in infinite dimensions', arXiv:2409.04028, submitted 6 September 2024. Proves a lower bound 𝐁*_X ≥ √3/4 for the Bloch constant of mappings F(x)=f(x)x on the unit ball of a complex Banach space (Theorem 3.14(ii)).
events.delivers: Lower bound √3/4 for a Bloch constant on mappings of the unit ball of a complex Banach space. Variant (infinite-dimensional); the paper states the classical disc constant has a higher known lower bound, √3/4 + 2·10⁻⁴, and does not improve it.
events.direction: Variant result, does not touch the classical constant.

events.what_happened: Y. He and Q. Tang, 'Generalizing the Clunie–Hayman construction in an Erdős maximum-term problem', arXiv:2602.12217, submitted 12 February 2026. Gives B > 0.58507 for the constant B of Erdős Problem 513, defined over transcendental entire functions as sup_f liminf_{r→∞} μ(r,f)/M(r,f). The paper says explicitly that it does not call this the Bloch constant. Disclosure: 'An AI assistant (ChatGPT, model: GPT-5.2 Pro) was used for exploratory brainstorming and to draft the initial version of the script cert_mesh_arb.py in Appendix A.' and 'All mathematical arguments and all code were subsequently checked and verified by the human authors.'
events.delivers: A lower bound for a different constant (maximum term of the Taylor series versus maximum modulus, for transcendental entire functions). Not a Bloch or Landau constant.

checked_by.who: The paper's human authors (Y. He, Q. Tang)
checked_by.qualification: Authors of the work; not an independent check
checked_by.what_they_did: State that all arguments and code were checked by the authors

events.direction: Variant result, does not cut against the classical conjectures.

events.what_happened: M. F. Ali and S. Azim, 'Bloch and Landau constants for meromorphic functions', arXiv:2603.05047, submitted 5 March 2026. Shows that the Bloch and Landau constants B(1), L(1) for meromorphic functions with a simple pole, and B(p), L(p) for p in (0,1), are infinite (Theorem 2.2). This refutes the conjecture of Bhowmik and Sen that Theorem A's bounds are the exact values for B(p), L(p).
events.delivers: For meromorphic functions in the class with a simple pole (and for A(p)), the Bloch and Landau constants are infinite. A variant class; says nothing about the classical holomorphic B or L.
events.direction: Variant class; the infinite values are a result about meromorphic functions, not holomorphic ones.

events.what_happened: The Erdős Problems site entry for Problem 513 (the constant B over transcendental entire functions) states: 'This was further improved slightly to 0.5850788 by GPT (as prompted by Sothanaphan).' The revision history shows this sentence first in the 2 April 2026 revisions (an earlier revision at 19:06:05 read 0.57850788; the 19:06:31 revision reads 0.5850788), and the 20 Oct 2025 revision has no GPT attribution. The attribution is the site's own text; I found no authors' account of how the figure was obtained.
events.revisions: Site revisions 20 Oct 2025 (no GPT attribution); 2 Apr 2026 19:06:05 (reads 0.57850788); 2 Apr 2026 19:06:31 (reads 0.5850788); current version (same figure).
events.delivers: Claimed improvement of the lower bound for the entire-function constant of Erdős Problem 513 to 0.5850788. A variant (not a Bloch or Landau constant), and the figure is unconfirmed by the authors of any paper.
events.doubts: Attribution is the site's text, not an authors' account. The figure differs by a digit between revisions (0.57850788 vs 0.5850788), which the site later corrected; 0.5850788 is consistent with He–Tang's 0.5850724.
events.direction: Variant constant; raises a lower bound on a non-Bloch quantity.

events.what_happened: F. Wikström, 'An improved lower bound for Bloch's constant', arXiv:2608.17660, submitted 18 August 2026 (v1, the only version listed). Proves B ≥ √3/4 + 0.0153 = 0.448312701… (Theorem 1.1), with an intermediate Proposition 1.2 giving B ≥ √3/4 + 0.0114402996202 = 0.44445300151…. The method refines Bonk's method, with a linear program over Bloch-class coefficients, a moment inequality |ν₃| ≤ 1 − |ν₂|², and a two-radius split, and every inequality is re-verified in interval arithmetic (Arb at 40 decimal digits, HiGHS via SciPy for the LPs). The paper states that the gap to the Ahlfors–Grunsky upper bound shrinks from 0.0385 to 0.0235.
events.revisions: v1 18 Aug 2026 only, per the arXiv abstract page as fetched.
events.delivers: A lower bound for the classical Bloch constant B (holomorphic f on the unit disk with f'(0)=1): B ≥ √3/4 + 0.0153 ≈ 0.448313. Lower bound only; no upper bound; no claim on the Ahlfors–Grunsky conjecture beyond the paper's stated shrinkage of the gap to 0.4718617….
events.remains: Part (a): exact value of B still open, with the conjectured value (Ahlfors–Grunsky upper bound ≈ 0.4718617) unchanged. Parts (b) and (c) are not addressed by this paper.

machine_checked.system: Arb ball arithmetic (40 decimal digits) with HiGHS linear programs; inequalities re-verified in interval arithmetic. Not a proof assistant; no Lean/Coq build found.

events.directly_checkable: The certificate is a finite linear-programming dual certificate over the Bloch-class coefficient inequalities, re-verifiable by re-running the interval-arithmetic scripts that the paper says are archived on Zenodo (DOI not obtained). Not checkable by hand from the text.
events.doubts: Unrefereed, sole author, no independent re-check found in any source. The paper's own AI-tool statement (see ai) says the models helped develop the verification scripts and audit proofs; the author states all material was reviewed. The baseline Xiong 1998 figure used for comparison was not checked by the author against the paper. No specific error has been identified by any source.
events.direction: Raises the lower bound on B towards the conjectured value; consistent with B being at most the Ahlfors–Grunsky upper bound; does not decide the exact value.

events.what_happened: F. Wikström, 'A computer-assisted lower bound for Landau's constant', arXiv:2609.23236, submitted 19 September 2026 (v1, the only version listed). States the lower bounds B∞ > 0.51 and L > 0.51. For L, the smallest certified radius is 0.51003 over a finite cover of the normalised coefficient body by 1179 boxes; all numerical premises verified with Arb at 80 decimal digits; floating-point linear programming used only to find dual vectors; an independent arbitrary-precision interval program reconstructs the witnesses. The paper cites Wikström's 2608.17660 as reference [12]. Also reports earlier certificates at 0.508 and 0.5088 available from the author.
events.revisions: v1 19 Sep 2026 only, per the arXiv abstract page as fetched.
events.delivers: A lower bound L > 0.51 for the classical Landau constant (part (b)). Also B∞ > 0.51 for the locally univalent Bloch constant, which is a variant and not the classical B; the paper does not bound the classical B. Lower bound only.
events.remains: Part (b): exact value of L still open, with the conjectured value (Rademacher's upper bound ≈ 0.5432589) unchanged. Part (a) (classical B) not addressed by this paper. Part (c) (A) not addressed.

events.directly_checkable: A finite interval-arithmetic certificate over 1179 boxes covering the normalised coefficient body; checkable by re-running the programs archived at Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22849858, as cited in the HTML rendering), not by hand.

events.direction: Raises the lower bound on L towards the conjectured value 0.5432589…; does not decide it. The B∞ bound is a variant and cuts nowhere in the classical question.
events.object: No counterexample. The result is a finite interval-arithmetic certificate: a cover of the normalised coefficient body by 1179 boxes with smallest certified radius 0.51003…, from which L > 0.51 follows.

disputes.summary: Prior record for the classical Landau constant L: Eremenko's Purdue notes, a 2023 Canadian Mathematical Bulletin paper and a 2026 survey snippet give 1/2 + 10⁻³³⁵ (Yanagihara 1995). Wikström's arXiv 2609.23236 assigns 1/2 + 10⁻⁴¹⁷ to Yanagihara for B∞ and 1/2 + 2·10⁻⁸ to Chen–Shiba for B∞; its abstract says it improves 'the earlier bound of 1/2 + 2·10⁻⁸ due to Chen and Shiba'. Not resolved; the 0.51 result exceeds all of these figures, so the dispute does not change the 2026 bound.

Xiong (1998): Wikström's introduction gives B ≥ √3/4 + 3·10⁻⁴ (value taken from MathSciNet and zbMath, paper not obtained); MathWorld lists Xiong 1998 among refinements of the 2·10⁻⁴ bound attributed to Chen–Gauthier.

Who conjectured the exact value of the Landau constant upper bound: the Bloch-theorem Wikipedia article credits Ahlfors and Grunsky with conjecturing that their upper bounds are the exact values of B and L; MathWorld credits Rademacher (1943), after Robinson (1938, unpublished), and says Rademacher conjectured equality for the Γ(1/3)Γ(5/6)/Γ(1/6) bound. The record gives both.

Which constant the Yanagihara 10⁻³³⁵ and 10⁻⁴¹⁷ bounds concern, and which constant the Chen–Shiba 2·10⁻⁸ bound concerns, differs between the Wikström 2026 introduction and other sources (see the two items above). Recorded, not resolved.

summary: The problem is 'What is the exact value of Landau's constants, including Bloch's constant?' with the constants read as the classical Bloch constant B, the classical Landau constant L, and (as a flagged reading of 'Landau's constants') the univalent constant A. Neither exact value is known as of 13 Oct 2026. Two in-window events move a named quantity and are recorded in full: Wikström's arXiv 2608.17660 (18 Aug 2026) raises the lower bound on B from √3/4 + 2·10⁻⁴ to √3/4 + 0.0153 ≈ 0.448313, with an intermediate √3/4 + 0.0114403; and Wikström's arXiv 2609.23236 (19 Sep 2026) gives L > 0.51 (certified radius 0.51003 over 1179 boxes), with a locally univalent variant B∞ > 0.51 that is not the classical B. Both are single-author, unrefereed, computer-assisted interval-arithmetic certificates; both carry an AI-tool statement; I found no independent public engagement with either and no later paper other than the second citing the first (same author). I read both through arXiv HTML renderings because the PDFs returned compressed streams; the verbatim quotes come from that rendering, and the 2609.23236 disclosure was returned as segments, so the middle clause is not verbatim. Close calls. (i) Scope: the Bloch result is about the classical constant the bullet names, so I treated it as in scope; the Landau result is in scope only if L is part of 'Landau's constants', which I think it is. (ii) AI: both papers state that OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code were used for mathematical brainstorming, proof auditing, numerical exploration and writing the verification scripts, and that the author reviewed the output. The Bloch paper names GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5.0; the Landau paper, a month later in the same series, names GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1. Those are the strings each paper uses; I did not reconcile them, and did not date the models. Whether any of this is load-bearing is not stated by either paper; the papers say which uses they had, not which ideas came from the models. (iii) Variants recorded and discarded from the classical question: the meromorphic infinite-constant result (Ali–Azim 2026), the elliptic-harmonic result (Bhowmik–Sen 2024), the infinite-dimensional result (Hamada–Kohr–Kohr 2024), and the entire-function constant of Erdős Problem 513 (He–Tang 2026, with a ChatGPT GPT-5.2 Pro disclosure; the 0.5850788 figure on the Erdős site is attributed to GPT by the site alone, not by authors). The pre-window bound history is recorded from the reference lists of the 2026 papers and MathWorld, and most of the primary historical papers were not opened. The Wikipedia Bloch-theorem article as fetched still gives 0.4332 ≤ B ≤ 0.4719 with Chen–Gauthier as the lower-bound source, so the encyclopedia has not picked up the 2026 bounds; ProofWiki likewise. Carroll–Ortega-Cerdà (2008/2009) improved the upper bound on the univalent constant A to about 0.6564, where the Wikipedia-style text still says 0.7853.
competing_reading: Read through the authors' own tooling disclosures, the AI involvement in both Wikström papers is peripheral. The stated uses (brainstorming, proof auditing, numerical exploration, writing verification scripts) are work around the mathematics. The bounds rest on Bonk's method and on finite certificates that the paper says are re-verified in interval arithmetic, so the mathematics is human-designed and machine-checked, and a judging pass could reasonably count neither as AI-produced mathematics. Read the other way, the disclosure says the models were used for 'brainstorming', which in a paper whose only new content is an LP design and a moment inequality could mean the design came from the models; the paper does not say which ideas originated where, so the involvement cannot be excluded as load-bearing on the text alone.
what_would_settle_it: For AI: the author's account of which steps (the LP design, the moment inequality |ν₃| ≤ 1 − |ν₂|², the two-radius split, the 1179-box subdivision) originated with the models, and the Zenodo archive's commit history showing who wrote what. For the bound: an independent re-run of the archived interval-arithmetic certificates in a second library, or a referee report or journal acceptance. For the attribution conflicts: the original Yanagihara (1995) and Chen–Shiba papers, and Eremenko's notes with a date.
